subject: research/inertia-twin
professional: a robotics dynamics / simulation-fidelity engineer (someone who builds and validates rigid-body simulators or identifies inertial parameters for wheeled and legged robots, and refereed sim-to-real work). First checks: whether the stick/slip contact model is right, whether the 'twin' is a fair strawman of any real simulator, whether the result is anything beyond I = k m r^2 in an intro mechanics text, and whether it was checked against a physics engine or a physical body.

evidence.correctness: Ran `cd research/inertia-twin; PYTHONPATH=src python3 experiments/run.py > scratch; diff scratch experiments/results.txt`: byte-identical, so results.txt is current. Recomputed with a scratch script that does not import inertia_twin: (1) energy method m g L sin a = 1/2 m v^2 (1+k): a = 3.5036 / 3.2700 / 2.4525 m/s^2 and 2 m fall times 1.0685 / 1.1060 / 1.2771 s for sphere/disc/hoop, matching table 1; (2) Newton-Euler threshold mu* = k tan(a)/(1+k) at 5/30/45 deg: 0.0250,0.0292,0.0437 / 0.1650,0.1925,0.2887 / 0.2857,0.3333,0.5000, matching table 3; (3) coast: twin launch speed sqrt(2 g sin15deg) = 2.2534 m/s, stop distances (1+k)*1 m = 1.4/1.5/2.0, matching table 4; (4) calibration by independently written normal equations: c = 0.7143/0.6667/0.5/0.627 and cross-shape fall-time errors (0, -3.39, -16.33; 3.51, 0, -13.40; 19.52, 15.47, 0; pooled 6.74, 3.12, -10.70), all matching table 5; (5) slip regime, disc mu=0.1 at 30 deg, own semi-implicit integrator with dt 1e-3: v(1 s) = 4.05543 vs closed form 4.05543 vs the library's 4.0556. All headline numbers reproduce. Small discrepancy: the library's slip-regime result is 1.7e-4 m/s high (a real bug, see craft), inside the 3e-4 quoted tolerance. Not compared against a physics engine (MuJoCo, PyBullet), so 'the real system' is the author's own simulator, validated against closed forms only.
evidence.completeness: Claims checked: (1) twin overstates acceleration by exactly 1+k, 2 m fall 0.90 s vs 1.07-1.28 s: reproduced; (2) simulation matches g sin a/(1+k) to 3e-4: max diff in results.txt is 3e-4, yes; (3) slip threshold 0.1925 invisible to the twin: reproduced; (4) launch speed overshoot 40/50/100%: reproduced; (5) cross-shape calibration errors and 'twin cannot rank shapes': reproduced; '8 tests, under 1 s': `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` ran 8 tests, OK, 0.025 s; run.py about a second: ran, identical output. Files exist: experiments/ratio_vs_mu.svg, figure.py, paper/whitepaper.md, pyproject.toml. Live page https://marisstella.app/research/inertia-twin/ not loaded (egress proxy). No TODOs or stubs; Next steps (rolling resistance, reflected inertia, MuJoCo comparison, system identification of k) are declared undone. The planned physics-engine comparison, the one thing that would make it a sim-to-real study, is not done.
evidence.verification: `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`: 8 tests, OK. Tests compare the simulator against closed forms and check ratios and a sharp threshold at +-2%; reasonable but the closed forms and the simulator share the author's assumptions. Seeded 4 mutations in src/inertia_twin/model.py one at a time, ran the suite, reverted with `git checkout`: (1) f_roll (stick test) x1.2: caught (1 failure); (2) spin-up alpha = f/k -> f/(1.01 k): caught (1); (3) slip acceleration friction term x0.9 in accel_real: caught (2); (4) friction sign at zero slip `(1 if slip > 0 else -1)` -> `else 1`: NOT caught (OK). Mutation 4 is the place of a real defect (see craft): the correct sign at slip == 0 is not pinned down, and the tests' 2e-3 tolerance cannot see a 1.7e-4 offset. No test of a slip-to-roll transition during a run, nonzero launch slip, or negative-angle/zero-angle inputs. No regression test on results.txt. `git status` clean for the project after reverts.
evidence.craft: Read src/inertia_twin/model.py (about 80 lines), tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py (65 lines), pyproject.toml. Small, stdlib-only, clear docstrings, no copied engine. Defects: (1) in simulate(), when the body is released at rest in the slip regime (mu < mu*), slip == 0 on step 1 and the code uses `(1 if slip > 0 else -1)`, so friction points down-slope on the first step. I ran simulate(0.5, 30deg, 0.1, 1e-4): v = 5.75e-4 vs the correct 4.06e-4, w = -1.7e-4 (spinning the wrong way). The error persists: v(1 s) is 1.7e-4 m/s above the exact value (4.0556 vs 4.05543; my independent integrator matches the closed form). Small, but the code is wrong at the exact starting condition the experiments use; (2) s_eps = 1e-9 is an absolute slip tolerance, not scaled, and the stick test `abs(slip) <= s_eps` means a sliding body whose slip decays through zero is re-snapped only by the sign-change branch: untested; (3) the slip-to-roll snap uses a one-step momentum mix with no check against dt; (4) no input validation (mu < 0, a <= 0 gives division by zero in launch/coast functions, k <= 0); (5) run.py prints numbers with no assertions, agreement is read by eye; (6) `from inertia_twin.model import *` in tests and run.py.
evidence.claims: Each README/whitepaper claim was matched to a line of results.txt and reproduced (see completeness); the numbers quoted in prose (0.90 s vs 1.07-1.28 s, 0.1925, 40/50/100%, -16%..+20%, +6.7%..-10.7%, c = 0.714/0.667/0.500/0.627) all match. 'Stylised' is disclosed along with its reason (planar incline, Coulomb friction, no rolling resistance, textbook mechanics, no hardware data), and the whitepaper states 'Nothing here is a new physical result' and that results 1-3 are exact consequences of the equations. The 'Builds on' paragraph names HIRO, ARPG and RECUV as directions and says nothing is reproduced or endorsed. Minor: the README item (2) says simulation matches 'to 3e-4 m/s^2' while the slip-regime offset is 1.7e-4 from a bug rather than time-step error (still true). Whitepaper says 'a 2 m descent takes 0.903 s' (twin) consistent with table. No overclaim found; the live page was not loaded.
evidence.fitness: Research bar (research/CLAUDE.md): a PhD-level programme aimed at a publishable result. This is a one-session, ~80-line model of a solved textbook problem; the whitepaper itself says nothing is a new physical result. Nearest prior work: every intro mechanics text (Goldstein et al. cited; also Meriam and Kraige, Dynamics) for a = g sin a/(1+k) and the no-slip threshold; Atkeson, An and Hollerbach (1986) and Khalil and Dombre for inertial parameter identification in robots; Hwangbo et al. and Tan et al. (2018) and Zhao et al. (2020) on sim-to-real gap; reflected-inertia treatments in robot dynamics. 'A point mass ignores rotational inertia' is the standard sim-to-real example, so the result is sound but not new, and the headline effect is 1+k by construction (the twin is defined to have k = 0). The only mildly novel content is the cross-shape calibration table (one scalar gain cannot fix a mixed fleet), which follows in one line from the factor 1/(1+k) differing per shape. A researcher could reuse it as a unit-test fixture for a rigid-body engine, but there is no real data, no physics engine comparison and no programme behind it. Scored 1: a correct demo that a practitioner cannot build a paper on.
evidence.domain: A simulation/dynamics engineer would check: the Coulomb stick/slip logic (done as a clean friction-cone test, correct apart from the zero-slip sign defect above), the rolling constraint with I = k m r^2 (correct), and whether the 'twin' is a realistic baseline. Departures: (1) the baseline is a frictionless point mass, which no production simulator (MuJoCo, Bullet, Isaac, Gazebo-ODE) is: they model rotational inertia and Coulomb or pyramidal friction, so the gap they would have is contact-model and parameter error (friction cone approximation, restitution, solver slack), not a missing 1+k; (2) no rolling resistance or compliance, which dominates real coast distances: the 40/50/100% overshoot claim would be diluted by rolling resistance and drag that the sibling twins in the repo study separately; (3) the calibration experiment fits a scalar gain on the acceleration, whereas the standard remedy is to identify the inertia parameter k directly (the whitepaper lists it under Next steps; one descent gives 1+k exactly), which makes the 'one calibration cannot fix a fleet' result a strawman of practice; (4) no comparison to a physical body or to a reference engine. Method is correct but at textbook level.

defects.what: The result is a textbook identity (a = g sin a/(1+k), mu* = k tan a/(1+k)) against a twin defined to have no rotational inertia, so the headline is true by construction; no physics-engine comparison, no real data, no programme. Nearest prior work (Atkeson et al. 1986 parameter identification, sim-to-real surveys) is not cited for the calibration claim, and direct identification of k from one descent, the standard remedy, makes the scalar-gain failure a strawman.

simulate() applies friction in the wrong direction on the first step when released at rest in the slip regime (slip == 0 maps to sign -1): after one step v = 5.75e-4 vs 4.06e-4 and w = -1.7e-4; v stays 1.7e-4 m/s above the exact value afterwards. A seeded mutation of that sign was not caught by any test.

Tests use 2e-3 tolerances and no test covers a slip-to-roll transition during a run, nonzero launch slip, or invalid inputs (mu < 0, a <= 0, k <= 0); run.py has no assertions, so agreement with closed forms is read by eye.

verdict: Every number in the README and whitepaper reproduces and I recomputed five groups of them (energy method, Newton-Euler threshold, coast distances, calibration normal equations, an independent slip integrator) without the library; claims are honest and labelled stylised, so correctness, completeness and claims are at the bar. It fails the bar on verification (a seeded sign mutation at the zero-slip start survived, and that point hides a real if tiny bug: friction points the wrong way on step 1 in the slip regime) and, more importantly, on fitness: the finding is an intro-mechanics identity measured against a twin with no inertia by definition, with no physics-engine comparison or real data, and a calibration strawman. A robotics simulation engineer would call it a correct teaching note, not research.
